strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine challenges in personalized medicine under distribution shift
Principled mathematical framework with novel entropy-guided optimization formulation and rigorous derivations (Lemmas 4.2-4.3, Theorem D.1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 5 medical tasks with strong empirical results (average rank 1.2) against 10 baselines
Extensive ablation studies examining LLM choices, hyperparameters, knowledge quality, and design alternatives (12+ ablations)
Reproducible methodology with detailed algorithms, cost analysis ($0.21-0.60/patient), promised code release, and privacy-preserving design
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: Wasserstein constraints (Yao et al. 2024), LLM entropy uncertainty (Kuhn et al. 2023), and optimization-by-prompting (Yang et al. 2024) are from prior work; contribution is primarily in combination rather than introducing new concepts

Entirely simulation-based evaluation with artificially constructed distribution shifts and learned 'ground truth' oracles; no prospective clinical validation or real-world deployment, creating significant gap between evaluation and stated application

Strong dependence on prior knowledge quality with dramatic performance degradation under adversarial knowledge (Rank 5.0 vs 1.0, Table S5), and LLMs' known susceptibility to medical misinformation make practical guarantee of knowledge quality challenging

Best performance requires proprietary closed-source reasoning models (o4-Mini, Gemini-2.5 Flash); open-source models significantly underperform (Llama-3.1-8B Rank 6.2), creating privacy concerns and limiting practical deployment in healthcare
Marginal improvements on simpler tasks (Warfarin: 1.36 vs BO-qEI 1.36; HIV: 4.50 vs 4.53) with differences within error bounds; rank advantage primarily driven by Breast/Lung tasks

Theoretical assumptions not fully justified in practice: Lemma 4.2 assumes continuous, coercive functions but ˆf and c* are learned models without smoothness guarantees; Lemma 4.3 assumes convexity for non-convex problem

Ad-hoc equivalence relation via k-means clustering on text embeddings lacks principled justification; strong dependence on embedding model (Table S7) suggests fundamental uncertainty in design equivalence definition
Despite no-fine-tuning claims, method requires careful hyperparameter tuning (temperature τ, Wasserstein bound W₀, batch size) and hyperparameter sensitivity undermines practical applicability

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine clinical challenge: surrogate model generalization failures under patient population distribution shift
Theoretically principled approach with sound mathematical framework: properly derives Lemmas 4.2-4.3 and connects to Wasserstein distance theory with theoretical guarantees
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 5 real-world medical tasks, 10 baselines, convincing results (avg rank 1.2), outperforms human-prescribed treatments
Extensive ablation studies: 12 different ablations validating all major design choices including both constraints (λ and μ), embedding models, equivalence relations
Innovative knowledge integration: enables LLMs to leverage domain expertise via tool-calling without fine-tuning; quantitative analysis shows task-specific knowledge selection
Excellent reproducibility: full pseudocode, complete prompts, detailed hyperparameters, code availability promised
Appropriate ethical treatment: acknowledges LLM biases, correctly disclaims clinical use, discusses privacy implications
High technical quality: rigorous mathematical exposition, clear writing, comprehensive appendix with qualitative examples
weaknesses: Exclusively simulation-based evaluation without prospective clinical validation: distribution shifts are author-constructed, surrogate models learned from data—limits confidence in real clinical applicability

Critical dependence on prior knowledge quality: adversarial knowledge causes dramatic 35% performance drop (Breast: 72.74→47.67 TTNTD), requires expert knowledge vetting, creates deployment bottleneck
Significant LLM model dependency: closed-source models substantially outperform open-source (rank 3.0 vs 6.2), creates privacy concerns and API dependency
Hyperparameter sensitivity: temperature requires careful tuning (too low/high breaks method), W₀ shows peaked performance, somewhat contradicts 'no task-specific tuning' claims
Arbitrary equivalence relation definition: k-means clustering in embedding space lacks principled justification relative to mathematically derived optimization framework
Surrogate model still required: method improves generalization but doesn't eliminate need for surrogate training, which may be scarce in real clinical settings
Modest experimental scale: only 100 test patients per task, no formal statistical significance testing, some improvements near error bar overlap
Reflection step appears ad-hoc: important for performance (~6-7% impact) but lacks theoretical justification, contrasts with principled optimization derivation
Limited task diversity: all 5 tasks are drug dosing/treatment selection; ADR shows weaker performance, limiting generalizability claims
Computational deployment under-explored: inference latency not analyzed, real-time clinical feasibility unclear, local vs API deployment tradeoffs unresolved

strengths: Mathematically principled optimization framework with rigorous constrained formulation (Eq. 4) and tractable solution derivation (Lemmas 4.2-4.3)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 5 real-world medical tasks with strong empirical results (average rank 1.2 against 10 diverse baselines)
Extensive ablation studies (14 distinct ablations) demonstrating careful experimental work and sensitivity analysis
Novel integration of information-theoretic concepts (entropy, LLM certainty) with optimization theory for constraining LLM-based design
Strong reproducibility: code available, implementation details specified, datasets documented or accessible
Addresses important practical problem: surrogate model failure under distribution shift for under-represented populations
Acknowledges limitations and ethical concerns (biases, fairness, clinical limitations with explicit non-deployment disclaimer)
weaknesses: Severely limited clinical validation: all experiments use simulated ground-truth or retrospective data with no prospective clinical studies, expert clinician evaluation, or real-world deployment—undermines clinical impact claims

Critical and unresolved dependence on prior knowledge quality: Table S7 shows dramatic performance degradation with irrelevant knowledge; adversarial knowledge destroys performance; no solutions proposed for knowledge curation/validation in practice
Artificial distribution shifts: constructed via single-feature stratification (age, race, year); doesn't capture realistic multidimensional clinical OOD scenarios; unclear if results generalize

Limited core novelty: Wasserstein regularization from Yao et al. (2024), entropy-based LLM uncertainty from prior work; contribution is primarily combining established techniques rather than fundamental methodological advance

Incomplete baseline comparisons: medical LLMs (MedPaLM, Med-RLVR) excluded with justification that structured outputs fail; Table S4 shows OPRO+Knowledge achieves comparable rank (2.8 vs 1.8), suggesting knowledge incorporation drives much improvement

Equivalence relation design appears ad-hoc: embedding model choice significantly affects performance (Table S9: random rank 5.0 vs Bio+Clinical BERT rank 1.2); no principled guidance for defining equivalence relations; connection to medical similarity unclear

Mathematical assumptions not verified: Lemma 4.2 continuity and coercivity assumptions not checked for actual surrogates; Lipschitz enforcement via parameter clipping appears arbitrary; linear regression μ estimation (Eq. 9) uses only N data points (high variance)

Hyperparameter sensitivity and poor practical guidance: multiple critical hyperparameters (τ, W₀, batch size, N) show significant sensitivity; temperature ablation (E.3) shows many τ values produce invalid outputs; limited guidance for tuning on new tasks

Limited evaluation scope: only single proposal evaluated (Table S11 shows LEON underperforms when k>1 proposals allowed); surrogate model quality/types vary without sensitivity analysis; some tasks use unrealistic 'exact' ground truth
Inadequate fairness analysis: limited to gender and race; subgroups sometimes too small (N_Male=5); no mitigation strategies proposed; analysis doesn't cover disease type or treatment complexity
